articles.title: Saudi Arabia strikes key fuel depot in Yemen as conflict with Houthis escalates
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia said Tuesday it had attacked a key fuel depot being used by Yemen’s Houthi rebels to support strikes on the kingdom’s airports and energy facilities, hours before the Iran-aligned group renewed their attacks on Riyadh and the southern region with missiles and drones.
articles.body: Saudi Arabia said Tuesday it had attacked a key fuel depot being used by Yemen’s Houthi rebels to support strikes on the kingdom’s airports and energy facilities, hours before the Iran-aligned group renewed their attacks on Riyadh and the southern region with missiles and drones. In the latest escalation between the two sides — which follows a week of Houthi missile and drone attacks that killed at least 20 people and shut Riyadh’s main international airport — Saudi forces said they had struck Al-Sabaha Central Station, the rebels’ largest fuel distribution hub in northern Yemen, with a storage capacity of about 58,000 metric tonnes. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen claimed the Houthis were using the facility to support military operations that target sites inside the kingdom and against commercial shipping in the Red Sea. The operation came despite an earlier statement from the Houthi-controlled Yemen Oil Company that the facility held no stocks of petroleum products and that an attack would not affect fuel reserves or supplies. The strikes killed two civilians and injured two, according to the Houthis, though the Saudi-led coalition insisted it had warned civilians to leave the area beforehand. “This operation focused on neutralizing the capabilities the Houthi militia uses to threaten the kingdom, Yemen, the southern Red Sea and maritime corridors,” coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said in a statement. Hours later, in what appeared to be a Houthi response, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed three cruise missiles and two drones targeting the Riyadh region and southern Saudi Arabia. At least four people were injured from falling debris, according to Saudi authorities. Meanwhile, an administrative building belonging to the state oil giant Aramco in the Eastern Province city of Dhahran was also targeted, causing a limited fire. The Energy Ministry said no injuries were reported. Tuesday’s exchange comes amid signs the long-running conflict, which reignited this summer and intensified last month after years of relative calm, is continuing to escalate. Earlier Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile launched toward its eastern province, and another aimed at Haradh near the Yemeni border. It also reported intercepting three Houthi drones north of Riyadh. Meanwhile, Houthi-run Al Masirah TV reported that artillery fire by the Saudi-led coalition in Saada province wounded three Yemenis and two African residents in Baqim district. It later reported that two civilians were killed and two others wounded by artillery fire on residential villages in the border district of Shada in Sadaa, and also reported strikes in Sanaa and several other provinces. CNN cannot independently verify the reports. The conflict has been intensifying since the Houthis announced in July that — in response to what they say is retaliation for a Saudi blockade on the Yemeni capital — they would target Saudi shipping in the Red Sea as well as infrastructure inside the kingdom. Those attacks have stepped up in recent days, including with repeated strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, where 13 people were killed and more than 300 wounded on Saturday in what was the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. The US, UK, Spain and Canada are among countries now warning their citizens against using the airport. Meanwhile, the US State Department on Tuesday expanded travel restrictions for US government personnel in the kingdom, saying employees now require special authorization from the chief of mission to use any airport in Saudi Arabia. The attacks have also exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom’s defense capabilities as it wages its air campaign in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which is fighting the Houthis on the ground. On Tuesday, the Yemeni government forces claimed to have made continued advances in the military operation, dubbed “Dawn of Yemen.” It said that in the past 24 hours its forces had carried out 2,200 strikes against Houthi positions, killing about 1,200 fighters and destroying or disabling more than 440 military vehicles and other assets. CNN could not independently verify the figures. Meanwhile, the Houthis vowed further attacks against economic and aviation targets within Saudi Arabia, warning that they would target facilities belonging to the state-owned oil company Aramco as well as the King Khalid International Airport if Saudi forces continued attacking them.

articles.title: Mauritius imposes curfew after night of unrest over police shooting
articles.summary: Protesters block roads and burn tyres in response to a police shooting of a 27-year-old woman.
articles.body:
Mauritius has announced a curfew in parts of the country after the shooting of a woman by a police officer prompted public unrest overnight.

Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam said the curfew would take effect from 8:30pm local time (16:30 GMT) and last until 6am (02:00 GMT) in an address to the nation on Tuesday.

Some schools were closed on Tuesday on the Indian Ocean island due to the turmoil, according to the Education Ministry.

The curfew affects the capital Port Louis and major population centres on the popular island tourist destination, where public unrest is uncommon.

Local media reported that a police sergeant was charged in connection with the shooting of 27-year-old Elodie Thomas but did not provide details on what led to the incident.

Thomas was wounded in the south of the country’s capital while travelling home from work in a van. The Health Ministry said Thomas underwent a successful surgery to remove a bullet.

On Monday, protestors burned tyres and blocked roads in response to the shooting, which led to police deployments. The prime minister’s office said the situation had returned to normal and the public sector would operate as usual following unrest overnight.

According to the Reuters news agency, Mauritian police said an investigation into the incident is currently underway. Ramgoolam’s cabinet is reportedly set to meet on Wednesday to assess the situation.

articles.title: NYC socialist candidate says criminal record of man shot by ICE 'doesn't even matter'
articles.summary: Democratic congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier told Hasan Piker that Oscar Belgal's criminal record "doesn't even matter" after he was wounded in an ICE shooting.
articles.body: New York Democratic congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier told Twitch streamer Hasan Piker Saturday it "doesn't even matter" that a man wounded in a shooting by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer had a criminal record. Chevalier's comments came after Oscar Belgal, a 28-year-old Dominican Republic national who the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) says is in the country illegally, was shot by an ICE officer during a targeted operation to arrest him. DHS said Belgal refused to comply with officers' lawful orders. Piker and Chevalier took issue with both New York and federal authorities highlighting Belgal's criminal history, arguing that his past crimes did not justify the use of force. MAMDANI DEMANDS TRUMP RELEASE ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SHOT BY ICE AGENT AS PROTESTS ERUPT IN THE BRONX During the encounter, Belgal pulled his vehicle forward before at least one officer fired seven rounds, striking him below his left ear, NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said at a news conference near the shooting site late Thursday. Tisch also said Belgal had two prior arrests, including for robbery and the criminal sale of a controlled substance. According to DHS, Belgal has a prior grand larceny conviction and previous arrests for assault, robbery, drug possession and weapons possession. Federal authorities also said he has ties to the notorious Trinitarios street gang. "What is the rap sheet for this person that Jessica Tisch is alleging is this criminal, and that the ICE apprehension was valid from that perspective?" Piker asked. "You know, I was just so angry as I was listening to it," Chevalier said. "I have gone back to her remarks to make sure that I was correct in our statement about it. But to me, it doesn’t even matter, right? It doesn’t even matter." MAMDANI CALLS ICE A 'ROGUE' AGENCY AFTER NYC SHOOTING, CLAIMS AGENTS VIEW LAW AS 'MERELY A SUGGESTION' Piker added that even if Belgal committed violent crimes like murder, it would not justify the ICE shooting. Chevalier also criticized Tisch for attempting to "villainize" Belgal. "Police Commissioner Tisch came out, and I understand that it is her role to provide more information, and that is why she comes to these press conferences. But rather than condemn ICE, rather than condemn the shooting or the events that had just taken place, she started to villainize Oscar, right? Villainize him, and, by extension, villainize anyone who was in his position," Chevalier said. Fox News Digital reached out to Chevalier's campaign for comment but did not immediately receive a response. An NYPD spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "The Police commissioner was giving a factual update on the incident, and we always provide criminal history in incident updates if we have it. It’s also one of the first questions that every media outlet asks the NYPD." HARRY STYLES ADDRESSES ICE SHOOTING IN NEW YORK WITH CALL FOR ‘DIGNITY AND JUSTICE’ The New York State Republican Committee criticized Chevalier's comments, calling them "further proof" that the Democratic Party has fallen. "The facts of this case are clear: An illegal immigrant and known gang member resisted arrest and was met with lawful use of force from our brave ICE agents," NY GOP communications director David Laska told Fox News Digital. "The new face of the Democratic Party went on a podcast hosted by a radical who believes America deserved 9/11 to openly side with the illegal immigrant gang member — further proof that today’s Democratic Party is extremist and anti-American to its core. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Americans will remember when we cast our ballots in November."

articles.title: Jantar Mantar denotification vindictive, vow to fight: Opposition
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A day after its mega SC march in Delhi, the united opposition on Tuesday lashed out at Modi govt for denotifying Jantar Mantar as a protest
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A day after its mega SC march in Delhi, the united opposition on Tuesday lashed out at Modi govt for denotifying Jantar Mantar as a protest site, accusing it of hatching a conspiracy to push protests to Delhi's fringes. The opposition vowed that the fight to "restore democracy" will continue, while warning that farmer and worker organisations will join the agitation soon."We have extreme respect for SC, CJI and the judicial system. They have a role to play, we hope they will play that role. But we are political people. Irrespective of what happens, which institution plays a role or not, people's resistance will continue," leader of the opposition in Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, said.At a tea hosted by Rahul for INDIA bloc members, they argued that they should challenge govt's 'Jantar-Mantar-not-for-protest' decision. They termed it a "vindictive" step.Elated over turnout for SC march, it was felt that the momentum should be sustained, though specific plans were not spelt out, especially in view of festive season. In the informal discussion, Rahul told allies to keep political organisations on "alert mode" for quick agitational action, like in 24 hours.Besides in the scheduled Nov 1 rally, there could be improvised programmes like mock parliament to remove CEC. They felt with the bloc becoming more agitation-oriented, ties with civil society are growing stronger, which must continue.They felt with the bloc becoming more agitation-oriented, ties with civil society are growing stronger, which should continue.The gathering included Congress's Sonia Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge, RJD's Tejashwi Yadav and Manoj Jha, SP's Harendra Malik and Anand Bhadauria, CPI-ML's Dipankar Bhattacharya, NCP's Supriya Sule, Sena UBT's Sanjay Raut, Mamata TMC's Sagarika Ghose, JMM's Mahua Maji, CPM's MA Baby, CPI's D Raja and Sandosh Kumar, VCK's Thol Thirumavalavan, RSP's NK Premachandran, Prashant Bhushan, Yogendra Yadav, AISA chief Neha Bora, and Sai Balaji, among others. Congress state in-charges, civil society and student representatives were also present.Rahul said govt has decided Jantar Mantar can no longer be used to express feelings for democracy. "We will challenge that idea, and it won't be so simple for govt to decide that Indians will not fight for their voice."MA Baby said govt has not only committed "vote theft, but also theft of protest site" while Rahul stressed "all protests are one". He said "net is closing" on PM Modi, Union minister Amit Shah, and CEC Gyanesh Kumar.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Royal Mail losing 400 postal workers a week, says union
articles.summary: The CWU says more posties are leaving since a new delivery system was brought in, that it claims is not working in hundreds of offices.
articles.body:
About 400 postmen and women are leaving Royal Mail per week, according to the Communication Workers Union (CWU), who claims this number has gone up since the company introduced a new delivery system earlier this year.

The CWU says the firm had been losing about 330 postal staff a week from a workforce of 83,000 before it rolled out DM26, which reorganised routes to improve delivery performance.

The union claims the new system is not working in hundreds of offices, and BBC Your Voice has heard from staff warning of a "nightmare" Christmas ahead as the number of parcels increases.

Royal Mail says the reforms are part of its plan to deliver a more "efficient and financially sustainable" service.

Over the last year we've been in touch with more than 30 postal staff in all four nations of the UK, as they have switched over to DM26.

It allows for second class post to only be delivered every other weekday, and is supposed to guarantee first class mail and parcels are delivered every day, by putting workers into groups of three and changing the walking pattern of rounds.

But posties speaking to us anonymously say parcels are still being prioritised, letters left behind, and time wasted in sorting and dividing mail into first and second class.

"I didn't take any first class mail out on my last shift because I was on a road that's been behind for weeks," a worker in the West Midlands told me. "But I'm sure a manager would have ticked a box to say all first class mail went out."

A Royal Mail spokesperson said the company always worked to ensure all mail - both letters and parcels - were delivered on time.

Only three-quarters of first class mail delivered on time

Royal Mail letters sit undelivered 'for weeks' as parcels prioritised, staff say

Some postal workers we've spoken to say the new model is also increasing their workload.

We asked eight workers in different areas to track their average step counts. Since the switchover all their steps increased by a quarter or even a third, often up to around 25,000 steps a day.

Several fear this Christmas will be a "nightmare".

"We all think this Christmas will be the worst ever, for us and our customers," said one postman in the East Midlands.

Bryn Dymott delivered post in the village of Wootton in Bedfordshire for nine years. For the most part he loved the job. But he left the company in July saying he couldn't face another "shambolic" Christmas.

"People put things in the post for them to be delivered, not for them to be delayed because Royal Mail hasn't got the systems in place and enough people to get them delivered."

Bryn says he wanted to speak out after leaving the company because he was sick of the fact that posties aren't able to say what's really happening.

He says the company is "proving it's impossible to have four people's work done by three people. It shouldn't really come as a surprise."

So far DM26 has been introduced in about 1,000 of Royal Mail's 1,200 delivery offices.

Now the CWU has told its members to pause further roll-out of the new system until a plan can be agreed with Royal Mail to address problems.

The union says that while it is operating successfully in around 500 offices, it has run into significant problems in hundreds of others.

"Put simply, if a boat is already taking on water, adding more passengers is unlikely to solve the problem," says Martin Walsh of the CWU.

The union said most Royal Mail workers leaving the company were believed to be new starters on part-time contracts, but also said there had been an increase in staff on legacy contracts departing.

Royal Mail, on the other hand, says the new system is on track to be up and running in all offices by Christmas.

It says the roll-out is 90% complete and that it is now delivering to "95% of addresses every day across the UK, up from 88% before the roll-out. The roll-out continues across our network and we expect quality of service to improve as deployment progresses."

The company says it is hiring, as usual, an additional 22,000 temporary workers over the Christmas period.

Royal Mail has battled with increased competition and falling demand for letter deliveries in recent years, and last week announced plans to cut 2,500 head office and other supporting roles by the end of 2027.

The company has also faced years of criticism from politicians and the public over slow letter deliveries - something which has continued since the new system has been rolled out.

The regulator Ofcom has fined Royal Mail more than £37m in the last three years for missing delivery targets.

But some MPs think it is time for a new approach, and a group of them will meet the regulator later on Wednesday.

"We need to think outside the box," Dave Robertson, Labour MP for Lichfield, Burntwood and the Villages in Staffordshire.

"We need to bring as many people to the table on this to make sure we come up with a long-term solution because what's been tried up to now clearly isn't working."

An Ofcom spokesperson said not only has it issued fines to Royal Mail in recent years but it has also demanded an improvement plan and reformed the obligations imposed on the company, adding: "We will continue to hold it to account using the full extent of the powers available to us."

Postal Services Minister Kate Dearden said Royal Mail's improvement plan was "a step in the right direction, but it must deliver tangible improvements for customers. We will continue to hold them to account on their performance."

articles.title: Is it OK for jobseekers or employers to use AI?
articles.summary: Graduates are increasingly using AI to misrepresent themselves in job applications, research suggests. But some say their peer group has no choice.
articles.body:
Would you use AI to help you write a CV or cover letter? How about during an online assessment or video interview for a job?

We are increasingly using the technology to help us with job applications, graduates and recruiters say, with many employers happy for us to do so within reason.

But when does it cross a line from being acceptable to unethical, or even cheating?

Tom, 22, from Maidstone graduated last year with a geography degree and says he applied for over 200 jobs before finally landing a role last month as a restaurant manager.

He says the process was "exhausting" and "demoralising", with employers often not even getting back to him, and he wouldn't have got through it without some help from AI.

"Employers want you to put your absolute best into the application, but if I'm applying for 10 to 20 jobs in a day, the reality is you can't do that."

While Tom says he never used the technology in an assessment or interview, he did use it to help him with cover letters and CVs or to find the right "buzz words" that early stage screening in a recruitment process will pick up on.

He also thinks it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen candidates .

"That's where it feels like a weird tightrope. You can't use AI too much because otherwise you're not human. But if you don't write like an AI, you may get skipped by the AI screening."

This summer, the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) surveyed 155 of the UK's biggest graduate employers and found they were becoming "more accepting" of candidates using AI during recruitment "at some stages of the recruitment process".

According to the trade group, the most commonly accepted use was writing cover letters or CVs, followed by completing online application questions.

However, it also found some 92% of employers had encountered or suspected AI "misconduct" in the job selection process - up from 85% last year. Most commonly this included using AI as a real-time assistant during online video interviews or to complete online assessments.

On top of this, the tech is also helping candidates write multiple applications at the same time - something known in the industry as "spray and pray". And Stephen Isherwood, joint chief executive of the ISE, says it is "driving up the competition and pressure on students" in an already competitive graduate recruitment market.

Hollie Moody, head of early careers recruitment at energy giant EDF, says she doesn't blame graduates for using AI in applications given how "brutal" the jobs market is right now. But she does think it's becoming a problem.

EDF opened its graduate recruitment scheme three weeks ago, but took the decision to close it early after receiving 12,000 applications - a 10% increase on last year.

Moody says AI almost certainly contributed to this, adding that the tech is being used "a lot more freely" in the actual selection process.

"What we don't have is a level playing field, because what you'll find is that some candidates will absolutely use AI throughout the whole process, and other candidates won't."

Like many firms, EDF now issues guidance on the appropriate use of AI in job applications, and is trying to make its recruitment process as "AI-proof" as possible.

It only reads CVs in the later stages of the hiring process and uses skills and behaviour-based online assessments and video interviews to better assess candidates' skills.

But Moody says some applicants still try to bend the rules, particularly in video interviews.

"A lot of the answers [we hear] are the same. Or people might pause whilst they wait for AI to come back to them with an answer. It's almost like people are reading a script."

AI job application rise 'risks hiring incapable staff'

AI era 'not all doom and gloom' for graduates, say analysts

Young jobseekers 'discouraged' by ghosting and AI

One recently employed trainee accountant, who didn't want us to use his real name, told the BBC he'd applied for 50 graduate jobs and used AI in every application. But he says it was only for researching roles, tidying up his CV and generating mock practise questions for video interviews.

While he says he would never use the tech to cheat on assessments he knows people who would.

"I know people who have applied for 100 jobs and after a while they become desperate. If they see everyone else is using AI, they think how can I compete?"

According to the ISE, the graduate market has stabilised after a sharp fall last year but remains tough. Graduate roles currently attract an average of 141 applications each, it says.

And while only 16% of employers it surveyed are using AI to screen candidates, more than half plan to introduce it due to the large volumes of applications they are receiving.

EDF does not currently use AI screening but Hollie Moody says they may have to in future.

She says the use of AI in job applications is a "moral dilemma" that employers and employees will continue to grapple with. But she stresses it cannot replace what her firm is looking for in new recruits.

"It's about authenticity, but also personality. We want diversity of thought in the business."

articles.title: Rahul Gandhi peddling lies on SIR to cover Congress poll defeats: Amit Shah
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Going on the offensive amid opposition's stir against special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, Union home minister Amit Shah
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Going on the offensive amid opposition's stir against special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, Union home minister Amit Shah Tuesday accused Rahul Gandhi of fabricating lies about the exercise to hide his failure resulting in a string of Congress defeats, and to protect "infiltrators" who have been registered as voters."You and not SIR is responsible for Congress's defeats. Since you emerged as the main leader of Congress and then became its president and the leader of opposition, Congress has continuously lost elections. You should introspect," he said, asking the main opposition party and its allies to prepare themselves for a fourth consecutive defeat in the 2029 Lok Sabha polls."In many states you have not been able to win election for decades," Shah said, citing Congress's barren electoral performance in a number of states, including in Gujarat, Tripura, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal, while SIR had started only after 2024.This is the first time Shah has taken on the opposition, which has been trying to ratchet up pressure for CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation through its street campaigns in the national capital, and signalled a determined intent of the BJP brass to challenge its opponents' allegation that Election Commission (EC) is working to benefit the party in polls.The framing of opposition's protests as an attempt to cover "infiltrators" is significant, as BJP has for long accused its opponents of helping illegal immigrants from Bangladesh as well as Rohingya from Myanmar getting registered as voters as part of their "votebank" politics.With opposition parties coming together, BJP and JD(U) held a joint press conference where Union minister Piyush Goyal dared opposition-run govts in different states to quit if it considered polls following SIR rigged.Union minister and JD(U) functionary Lalan Singh said the entire campaign is not for saving democracy but weakening it by targeting constitutional institutions and trying to stoke anarchy through street protests. The two ministers echoed Shah on Congress's poor show in UP, Bihar and Tamil Nadu for decades, and said it is not even a key party in vast swathes of the country.Shah: BJP victories in ballot paper civic polls lesson for RahulUnion home minister Amit Shah's sharp comments came after BJP notched up another facile win in three local body polls in Gujarat, leaving Congress far behind. Aam Aadmi Party lost deposits in all 32 seats it contested in Gandhinagar Municipal Corporation, he noted.This win coupled with BJP and its allies' similar impressive show in local body polls in Tripura and Rajasthan, besides in the recent assembly and LS bypolls, demonstrated that people of the country are standing with PM Modi, BJP, and NDA like a rock, Shah said.Many of these polls were held through ballot papers, he said, as the opposition has often blamed EVMs for its losses. "These elections are a lesson for Rahul Gandhi... You (Rahul) cannot win the confidence of people by fabricated media events, 'jhooth ki goonj'," Shah said, riffing on Rahul's "Chhatron ki Goonj" outreach to students in different cities.Mocking the opposition's march in New Delhi on Monday, he said Rahul Gandhi cannot become the voice of the people by mobilising cadres of 14 parties to collect a crowd of 8,000 through a distance of 1.5km. They have no reach in the vast hinterland, he added. "Your negative politics will not benefit you. You should connect with people," he added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Taking cognisance of allegations that women journalists were sexually harassed by police personnel while covering the Oct 10 protest for
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Taking cognisance of allegations that women journalists were sexually harassed by police personnel while covering the Oct 10 protest for resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar, Supreme Court Tuesday asked Delhi Police to depute a senior officer to the court on Thursday to respond to the charges.Senior advocate Indira Jaising said that 'Network of Women in Media' has filed a petition narrating the incidents of sexual harassment of women reporters during the anti-SIR protest on Saturday.When Jaising said she has already served an advance copy of the petition to solicitor general Tushar Mehta, who is representing Delhi Police, a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said, "We would like some senior police officer to remain present in the court to explain and assist the court."The day also saw senior advocate Gaurav Bhatia and Mahesh Jethmalani mentioning a petition seeking initiation of criminal contempt action against political leaders for storming SC on Monday evening and obstructing access to SC's petition filing counter, thus blocking the access to justice. The reference was clearly to leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and other INDIA bloc members who were part of a procession to SC on Monday.Bhatia and Jethmalani sought a ban on political activity inside the court's premises and preservation of CCTV footage of Monday evening.During an extraordinary hearing on Sunday - on the Oct 10 protest - SC had found authorities to have prima facie breached its Oct 9 order restraining complete closure of metro stations and train services in the capital on the day of protest.It had sought responses from Union home secretary, Delhi Police commissioner and Delhi Metro chief on contempt petitions filed against them. It had also sought a status report from police on petitions accusing use of excessive force on protesters, who were not allowed to assemble at Jantar Mantar.More journalists, senior advocate G Sankaranarayanan said, have filed contempt petitions, two of them, as well as a writ petition related to the protest. SC had directed that professional activities of lawyers, journalists and other professionals would not be hindered. He said the issues are serious.The CJI Kant-led bench said, "Of course all the issues raised in all the petitions are serious and we would like to examine them." On the alleged manhandling of advocates Shadan Farasat, Dinesh Dwivedi and Uttara Babar, a separate petition by lawyers was mentioned by senior advocate C U Singh.While a clutch of petitions were in favour of the street protest and castigating police action in not permitting protest at Jantar Mantar on Oct 10, there were a few stood out as they questioned the protest, its modus operandi and serious disruptions it caused in the city, hindering free movement of the silent majority and impeding their daily work.Given the rush of petitions to SC and the fact that Justice Mohana was attending court despite having fever, CJI Kant said all petitions would be taken for hearing Thursday. The bench also accepted the solicitor general's request for extension of time till Thursday for home secretary, Delhi Police commissioner and Delhi Metro chief to file their responses.Senior advocate Nithya Ramakrishnan, appearing for Apoorvanand Jha, alleged that students who were detained by police on Oct 10 were tortured in police custody.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Ex-gang leader gets 40 years to life for rapper Tupac Shakur’s 1996 murder
articles.summary: A 30-year hunt for justice ends with the sentencing of Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis, who has written about Shakur’s shooting.
articles.body:
A former gang leader accused of masterminding the 1996 drive-by shooting of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur has been sentenced to 40 years to life in prison.

Tuesday’s sentencing capped a 30-year-long cold case that rattled the golden era of rap music in the United States.

In August, Duane “Keffe D” Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, had been found guilty of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon.

Davis, 63, is the sole person charged in the death of Shakur, who died at the peak of his fame at age 25.

Judge Carli Kierny announced Davis’s sentence at a hearing in Las Vegas, Nevada, where she chided him for the murder.

“You don’t get to take a man from his family, you don’t get to take his very life, his whole future from him and just walk away from it, especially when that man is Tupac Shakur,” Kierny said. “The world never forgot about him and his death, and neither did Las Vegas.”

During the hearing, prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo said that whatever sentence the court imposes, Davis is “guaranteed to die” behind bars.

For nearly three decades, Shakur’s death remained one of the music industry’s most notorious unsolved mysteries, prompting endless debate over who did it and why.

Davis had long been a suspect, but investigators lacked evidence to pursue an indictment.

The investigative deadlock shattered after Davis publicly boasted about his involvement in media interviews. He also recounted his role in the murder in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend .

Previously, Davis entered into a 2008 proffer agreement with federal law enforcement officers, granting him limited immunity for statements he made privately to investigators.

But by repeating his statements outside his meetings with investigators, prosecutors said Davis had effectively voided the agreement’s protections.

DiGiacomo said that Davis was trying to profit from a killing that he committed, and for that, he deserves the maximum possible sentence.

Shakur had been in Las Vegas for a Mike Tyson heavyweight fight on the night of September 7, 1996, when he was shot.

Investigators said the shooting took place roughly two hours after a confrontation between Davis’s nephew, Orlando Anderson, and Shakur’s entourage.

In his memoir, Davis accused Shakur and his friends of assaulting his nephew. He explained he then sought to retaliate, and he admitted to handing the murder weapon to two alleged accomplices, seated in the backseat of a white Cadillac, who then fired the fatal shots.

Shakur had been in the passenger seat of a black BMW, stopped at a red light, when his vehicle came under fire. He died six days later.

Davis is the only person who was in the Cadillac that evening who is still alive.

Members of Shakur’s family spoke at the sentencing, including his siblings Maurice “Mopreme” Shakur and Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur.

“This man’s life mattered,” Sekyiwa Shakur told the court, while her brother called the murder “devastating, heartbreaking and sad”.

Following the verdict, Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal described the Shakur family as having to endure years of Davis “bragging about killing someone they loved”.

“They loved that man. And the arrogance that Mr Davis had in expressing his joy in killing that man ultimately was his undoing,” Palal said.

The ex-gang leader briefly addressed the court on Tuesday, asking the judge to order the return of property seized from his residence, including personal photographs.

When the judge asked if he wished to make any additional statements, Davis declined, stating, “No, I’m good.” He added that he would “appeal this case for sure”.

articles.title: Former Chicago police detective linked by DNA to 8-year-old girl's cold-case murder, police say
articles.summary: DNA evidence and a fingerprint linked Thomas F. McInerney Jr., a former Chicago police detective, to the 1960 cold case murder of Gloria Kowalewicz.
articles.body: A former Chicago homicide detective has been identified as the killer of an 8-year-old girl who disappeared while walking to church in 1960, with authorities now examining other cases that may have involved the officer. Thomas F. McInerney Jr. joined the Chicago Police Department in 1959, just one year before Gloria Kowalewicz was abducted and murdered. He later became a detective investigating violent crimes and remained with the department until retiring in 1987. More than 65 years after the killing, Chicago police confirmed to Fox News Digital that advances in DNA technology and a preserved fingerprint helped investigators identify McInerney, who died in 2006 at age 70. COLD CASE BREAKTHROUGH SOLVES TEEN KILLING AFTER SUSPECT LIVED FREE FOR DECADES: 'BETTER BE AFRAID' Gloria disappeared Nov. 12, 1960, after leaving her home shortly before 8 a.m. to attend morning Mass at St. Mary of Mt. Carmel Church, just a few blocks away. Her body was discovered roughly four hours later in a ditch at a forest preserve southwest of Chicago. She had been shot and killed. The murder prompted an extensive investigation, with police interviewing more than 1,300 people and knocking on hundreds of doors. Despite those efforts, the case remained unsolved for decades. Investigators preserved evidence from the crime scene and surrounding area, including a bullet, Gloria's coat and shoes, and a white communion purse containing her prayer book. A fingerprint was also recovered from the purse's strap. DISCARDED TRASH UNCAPS 41-YEAR-OLD MURDER CASE IN RITZY SEASIDE RESORT TOWN, AUTHORITIES SAY Working with the FBI and Illinois State Police, investigators used modern forensic technology to link DNA and the preserved fingerprint to McInerney, according to the department. "McInerney should never have worn the CPD star, and it is devastating to accept that he was never identified and held accountable while he was alive," Chicago police said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital. The Cook County State's Attorney's Office is working to identify other cases that may have involved McInerney, according to The Associated Press. KILLER EX-COP EXECUTED FOR CHILD'S SLAYING AS SHERIFF SAYS HE’S SURE SAME MONSTER MURDERED ANOTHER GIRL Police said Gloria's parents died before learning who killed their daughter, but expressed hope that identifying McInerney would bring some closure to those who knew her. McInerney later worked for the Federal Public Defender's Office in Nevada before retiring in 2004, according to the AP. He died two years later without facing charges in Gloria's murder. articles.title: Gales and heavy rain forecast for UK as Met Office wind warning issued
articles.summary: The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for wind in north-west Scotland on Wednesday with 70mph gusts possible, as Ben Rich explains.
articles.body:
A weather system containing the remnants of Hurricane Isaias is forecast to send gales, heavy rain and a surge of warm air to parts of the UK this week.

The centre of the low, and its most significant impacts, will stay hundreds of miles from UK shores but north-west Scotland will see a spell of gales.

A Met Office yellow warning has been issued for parts of the Highlands and Western Isles with the risk of gusts touching 70mph (113km/h) in places.

Heavy rain will also affect parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland but much of England and Wales will remain largely dry with spells of sunshine.

The area of low pressure will also send a renewed surge of warm air across the country bringing above-average temperatures for many.

Hurricane Isaias was the first Atlantic hurricane of the season and made landfall in the southern United States last Friday.

It weakened rapidly and ceased to be a hurricane but its remnants threw heavy rain across the eastern side of North America.

Since then, the leftovers have emerged over the Atlantic and been scooped up by a powerful jet stream .

This has developed a new area of low pressure that has been undergoing what meteorologists describe as explosive cyclogenesis, also referred to as a weather bomb .

The jet stream is steering the centre of the storm hundreds of miles away from our shores, passing close to Iceland where it will bring the threat of blizzards.

Wind gusts over the sea between Iceland and the Faroe Islands could exceed 110mph but nothing this severe is expected in the vicinity of the UK.

Where will the strongest winds be in the UK?

The far north-west of Scotland will bear the brunt of the winds.

A Met Office yellow weather warning is valid on Wednesday from 10:00 until 19:00 BST, and warns of a high risk of moderate impacts including disruption to rail, air and ferry transport, delays on roads and bridges - especially for high-sided vehicles - and possible short-term power cuts.

Widespread gusts of 50-60mph are likely with 70mph possible for exposed coasts and hills around the middle of the day.

Outside the warning area, Shetland is also anticipated to see 50mph gusts - although the risk of disruption here is less - and 40mph gusts are possible in other parts of Scotland, Northern Ireland, northern England and north-west Wales.

After a mainly dry start, outbreaks of rain are expected to arrive in many parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland by the end of the day, with heaviest rain in the north and west.

Some patchy rain may also spread into north-west England and north Wales, but most of both countries will stay fine with sunny spells after any early mist has cleared.

The deep area of low pressure is set to send warm south-westerly winds across the UK.

Temperatures will widely climb into the mid to high-teens Celsius, possibly peaking at 20C in a few locations in southern England.

This will leave most places 2-4C above the mid-October average.

This warmth will linger in many parts of England and Wales on Thursday with temperatures expected to peak at 22C in East Anglia.

However, a weather front will move slowly southwards taking rain across Scotland, Northern Ireland, northern England and north Wales and behind it things will start to turn cooler.

Those chillier - and eventually drier - conditions will then spread southwards across the UK through Friday and over the weekend.

Temperatures will fall much closer to the seasonal norm with brisk winds accentuating the colder feel around some eastern coasts and the chance of overnight frost in places.

Computer models suggest that high pressure will then settle close to the UK which should keep Atlantic low pressure systems at bay for the time being, bringing long spells of dry weather for many.

You can check your local weather prospects on the BBC Weather website and app .

articles.title: Man who lived as woman for eight years warns surprising teen sexuality data may not tell full story
articles.summary: Walt Heyer says social media and peer pressure may explain why fewer teenagers now identify as gay or bisexual, casting doubt on CDC data trends.
articles.body: A man who spent eight years identifying as a woman is casting doubt on reports of a dramatic decline in teenagers identifying as gay or bisexual, warning that social media and peer pressure may be influencing how young Americans describe their sexual orientation. Walt Heyer, who detransitioned roughly 40 years ago and now serves as a senior fellow at the Family Research Council, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive video interview he remains skeptical of the apparent shift, suggesting some teenagers may be reluctant to openly identify as gay or bisexual because of social pressures. "I don't really believe that there's a big dramatic free fall," Heyer said, referring to recent reports about declining rates of gay and bisexual identification among some teenagers. LOG CABIN REPUBLICANS REMOVES 'T' FROM LGBT ADVOCACY, SAYS 'RADICAL' TRANS ACTIVISTS ARE ERODING GAY SUPPORT "I think what's happening is that, because of social media, there's a lot more influence on people who may not want to fall into that classification on a social media level and will withhold the fact that they are gay or bisexual but really don't want to openly admit it," Heyer said. The comments come after The Washington Post highlighted CDC data showing that the percentage of ninth grade girls identifying as lesbian or bisexual fell from 30% in 2021 to 17% in 2025. The share identifying as bisexual alone dropped from 26% to 13% over the same period. PRISHA MOSELY: AS A DETRANSITIONER AND MOM, I KNOW WHAT GENDER IDEOLOGY STOLE FROM ME The percentage of boys identifying as gay or bisexual has remained largely unchanged over the past decade, while the share of high school girls identifying as lesbian or bisexual surged after the COVID-19 pandemic before beginning to decline, the Post reported. Heyer, an author and co-author of multiple books, including "Trans Life Survivors" and "Paper Genders," and has spent years working with people questioning their gender identities, argued that social dynamics among young people could complicate attempts to interpret the findings. "I've had actual people in school saying that they're bullied into identifying one way, or they're bullying and bullied to not identify that way," he said. BLUE STATE SCHOOL DISTRICT ACCUSED OF DEFYING SUPREME COURT, HIDING GENDER TRANSITIONS FROM PARENTS Heyer also said he believes peer and societal pressures are significant factors in kids choosing to identify with something else that is not their biological sex. "What's interesting about that is that many kids are sort of coerced by their peers to say things one way or the other, so I've been very skeptical about what the kids are saying, whether they're gay or bisexual," Heyer said. "I don't really believe that there's a big dramatic free fall. That was, I think, quoted as a free fall in the people identifying as gay or bisexual," he added. "I think what's happening is that, because of social media, there's a lot more influence on people who may not want to fall into that classification on a social media level and will withhold the fact that they are gay or bisexual but really don't want to openly admit it." A DETRANSITIONER CONFRONTED A CALIFORNIA LAWMAKER ON THE HARMS OF GENDER TRANSITION. HERE'S WHY HE SPOKE OUT Simply but perhaps most importantly, Heyer said he thinks adults should do a better job of only affirming what is true. "I think that what I've really discovered is that we know now and have evidence, factual evidence, that nobody has ever changed their gender," Heyer said. "I went through the hormones, had all the surgeries, identified that way. So far in all world history, nobody has actually biologically changed their gender. This is a cosmetic social appearance. It is not a biological change. "And when you come to that conclusion, you realize that really the procedures and these terminologies and labels, what I refer to as God rejecting labels, God rejecting procedures in every aspect. This is the way young people and adults reject God and say God doesn't exist by taking these labels on," he added. DETRANSITIONERS REVEAL HOW DOCTORS PUSHED THEM TOWARD LIFE-ALTERING TREATMENT AS TEENS Heyer also urged researchers to conduct additional studies before concluding that the numbers reflect a lasting shift in sexual identity. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I just think it's important for us to be much more thorough and go to other areas before we come to some conclusion that there's a giant, giant drop in these identities," he said. "I don't think we're there yet."

articles.title: Our memorial garden helps us grieve - a cemetery felt too far away
articles.summary: Emma Moore shares how creating a special place at home has helped her family.
articles.body:
When Emma Moore's daughter Mabel died, the idea of visiting her in a cemetery felt too far away.

"I don't like going to them and I feel like [visits] fizzle out," she says. "At first, you'll go regularly and then it'll start being once a year."

Mabel was born prematurely at 27 weeks in April, her lungs had not fully developed and she lived for just two days. Emma keeps Mabel's ashes next to a photograph of her tiny feet but she wanted a special place to feel close to her.

"So we created something in the garden... [to] always be reminded of her every day," she tells Morning Live .

The stillness of green spaces "can help us connect with memories" of loved ones, says Andy Langford, clinical director at Cruse Bereavement Support.

And there are ways to create a special place of calm to remember anyone you've lost - even if you don't have a garden or know much about plants.

"I'd never done anything like this before, so I had no clue about where to start," says Emma, 35, who lives near Bolton with her partner Louis and elder daughter Penelope.

She chose to dedicate a part of the garden with a willow tree to Mabel. "I've enjoyed doing the gardening and planting. It was nice to focus on something."

Of all the flowers the family have planted in Mabel's garden, Emma's favourite are the lilies.

White lilies are said to represent peace and are a traditional choice for acts of remembrance in the UK, says botanist James Wong of BBC Gardeners' Question Time .

The flowers are low maintenance and can last for decades in your garden, he says, and there are a number of varieties to suit your soil.

The colour of your flowers is a personal choice, adds Wong, so there is no need to "follow the rules" of British tradition with white lilies.

You may find soft pink, mauve and lilac relaxing, or you may find yellows and reds more vibrant and lift your mood.

Wong says smell helps people connect to nature and works in harmony with the sight of beautiful flowers to create a peaceful atmosphere.

Many rose varieties have a fragrance but Wong also suggests choosing plants with scented leaves for when flowers are not in bloom.

"If you were to plant something like a mint, a eucalyptus or a rose geranium - they have very strongly scented leaves and they're around for a long period of time."

He also suggests evergreen Italian cypresses, tall and thin plants more commonly used for commemoration in warmer climates, as they are capable of growing "perfectly well outdoors in the UK". They have a woody aroma likened to pine or juniper.

Wong also says chrysanthemums - "a classic funeral flower" in East Asian cultures - will also readily grow here. They have a herbal almost medicinal fragrance.

Emma has placed a bench with a plaque featuring Mabel's name near the willow tree. She often sits on the bench in the morning with a cup of tea.

"It's her little garden," says Emma. "It's a really personal space."

Langford says benches are common in public memorial gardens because they offer "a sense of permanence" and, on a practical level, help you take a break from the stresses and rigours of everyday life.

If you want to use plants to create a memorial space indoors on a balcony or window box, think about nearby seating for two which opens up the opportunity for conversation about your loved one.

If you don't have a garden, Wong suggests choosing commemorative house plants suited to warmer conditions.

The peace lily, native to the rainforests of Colombia, will "grow perfectly well indoors all year round" but should be kept in warm conditions with low levels of light.

Frangipanis are "incredibly popular [in] Southeast Asia" and grow well indoors provided they have a reasonable amount of space and are placed in bright, warm spaces all year.

In Mabel's memorial garden there is also a swing surrounded by planters full of flowers. It's a place that has given Emma comfort. "I feel like I'm still very much grieving but I can just go and sit there and think about her and reflect on things."

articles.title: 15% increase in hate crimes against Hindus in UK, home office data shows
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from London: There has been a 15% increase in religiously-motivated hate crimes targeting Hindus in Britain, UK home office data reveals.
articles.body: TOI correspondent from London: There has been a 15% increase in religiously-motivated hate crimes targeting Hindus in Britain, UK home office data reveals.Police recorded a total of 146,825 hate crimes in England and Wales between March 2025 and March this year. Religious hate crime rose by 13%.There was also a 15% increase in hate crimes targeting Muslims, a 10% increase targeting Jews, a 3% increase targeting Sikhs and a 24% increase targeting Christians.Public fear, alarm or distress offences were the most commonly recorded hate crimes targeting Muslims and Jews.Hindu Council UK managing director Anil Bhanot said that was not the case for Hindus who were experiencing an increase in serious physical assaults. He said the statistics do not represent the true picture as “many Hindus still choose to suffer in silence” if a hate crime is not a physical assault. “They don’t report them as they don’t feel the authorities will do anything,” he said. He added whilst there was govt funding Hindu temples can apply for to protect their security, “historically nothing has been awarded to them”.“Synagogues and mosques have dedicated protection schemes, while Hindu temples have none and must compete for a small share of general funding,” a spokesperson for INSIGHT UK, an advocacy group for British Hindus, said.The spokesperson pointed out the home office “written commentary” accompanying the statistics was only about Jews and Muslims, with no mention of Hindus, the UK’s third-largest religious group. “A 15% rise should not be left as a line in a table,” the spokesperson said. “Our anti-Hindu hate survey, to be published in Nov, had 2,688 responses, and every respondent had witnessed or experienced anti-Hindu hate, from physical violence and online harassment to temple vandalism and the misrepresentation of Hinduism in the media and education.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Israeli attacks kill one in Gaza, wound journalists in occupied West Bank
articles.summary: A year into the ceasefire, nearly two-thirds of Gaza is in Israeli hands and Netanyahu vows control of the West Bank.
articles.body:
An Israeli air strike on a vehicle in Gaza City has killed one person and wounded several others, emergency services told Al Jazeera, as Israeli attacks continue a year into the ceasefire.

The strike hit the Tuffah neighbourhood, in the city’s northeast, on Tuesday.

In az-Zawayda, central Gaza, a four-year-old boy, Osama Ahmed Abed, died of wounds from an Israeli attack three weeks ago, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.

His death brought the number of Palestinians killed in Gaza since October 7, 2023, to more than 74,382.

Gaza’s Civil Defence agency said it was deeply concerned about repeated forced displacement near the “Yellow Line”, the boundary to which Israeli troops withdrew under the October 2025 ceasefire.

It said “massive explosions” and “indiscriminate gunfire” by Israeli forces had damaged hundreds of displaced people’s tents and weakened homes hit earlier.

It appealed for urgent intervention to “halt this war against the civilian population”.

Al Jazeera’s maps show nearly two-thirds of Gaza is now under Israeli military control or subject to access restrictions. The “Yellow Line”, set under US President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan to end the war, was meant to mark where Israeli forces first pulled back, with further withdrawals to follow.

Israeli forces have instead seized more territory.

The US-backed Board of Peace marked the ceasefire’s anniversary with a post saying Trump’s leadership “ended a war that had no end in sight”.

At least 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the truce began, and no Palestinian technocratic administration is in place.

More than 80 percent of Gaza’s buildings have been destroyed or damaged.

In the occupied West Bank, Israeli attacks in Ramallah and el-Bireh wounded a child with live ammunition and left several Palestinians suffocating from tear gas, the Palestinian Ministry of Health said.

Palestine TV correspondent Khaled Mattawa was wounded in the hand by a sound bomb, and Sky News Arabia correspondent Firas Lutfi in the leg by shrapnel, Wafa reported.

Israeli forces also raided the offices of several Palestinian non-governmental organisations and the courtyard of the Palestine Medical Complex.

Al Jazeera’s Nida Ibrahim, reporting from Ramallah, said the attacks were “yet another step to undermine the Palestinian Authority”.

Human rights lawyer Muhammad Dahleh said Israel uses laws and military orders to shut down Palestinian rights groups, naming them “terrorist organisations based on privileged evidence” that is withheld from the groups and their lawyers.

Several were outlawed in 2021, and legal objections were rejected by Israeli military authorities, he said.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a video on X that Israel was “preparing for a scenario in which Palestinian Authority forces turn their guns against Israel in the West Bank”.

“There will be no Arab army west of the Jordan River. There will be the [Israeli military],” he said, adding that Israel would extend its control across the territory.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Leonardo da Vinci: "The beginnings and ends of shadow lie between the light and darkness and may be infinitely diminished...could not be understood in detail but for shadow"
articles.summary: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian painter, scientist, and engineer who is most popularly known for painting the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper.
articles.body: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian painter, scientist, and engineer who is most popularly known for painting the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper. But beyond this, he also reflected on profound thoughts and filled thousands of notebook pages with studies of anatomy, water, flight, optics, and light.And these books are a treasure trove of knowledge where many words of wisdom often resurface as inspiration today.He once weighed in on a profound thought that we value things for their bright side only, celebrate success, and hide failure. We post the good days on social media and skip the rest. But a lot of what gives life its shape and meaning remains in areas that we usually overlook.Let’s dig in to find out what he means.Quote of the dayThe beginnings and ends of shadow lie between the light and darkness and may be infinitely diminished and infinitely increased. Shadow is the means by which bodies display their form. The forms of bodies could not be understood in detail but for shadowWhat does the quote meanLeonardo said that shadow begins and ends somewhere between light and darkness, comparing which he said that life can be made weaker or stronger without limit. He also wrote that shadow is how bodies show their form, and that we could not understand the details of those forms without it.By saying this, he means that shadow is not simply "no light." It is a gradual fade, and we fail to see many details or features; this is how light behaves as it lands on them.This idea shaped his art. Leonardo became famous for soft, smoky transitions between light and dark. This can be seen in the gentle shading around the face in the Mona Lisa.These words come from the consolidation of the pages that da Vinci wrote, from the book, the Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci, an edition compiled by Jean Paul Richter. Leonardo wrote these words in Italian, in mirror script, so what we read as an English translation can differ slightly between translators, but the essence of his ideas has hardly aged.How are these words relevant today?Even today, photographers and filmmakers use shadow to create mood and depth, and a portrait with no shadows looks lifeless. Game designers and 3D artists spend huge effort on realistic shading, because a digital object without it looks fake.Similarly, in daily life, we also tend to want everything bright: perfect results, constant happiness, no mistakes. But our difficult moments give our experience its depth. A person who has never struggled has a flatter story, much like a face lit from every side, understanding that is often the beginning of wisdom.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: What we know about the man who died falling from a Six Flags rollercoaster
articles.summary: Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died on Monday after police say he was ejected from a ride at a Six Flags amusement park in Georgia.
articles.body:
Warning: This story includes distressing content

A man has died after falling from a rollercoaster at a Six Flags amusement park on Monday in the US state of Georgia.

The man, Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, was found dead under the ride after being ejected and hitting other people on it, according to police.

An investigation is under way and few details have yet to be released about what happened. Six Flags, the largest amusement park operator in North America, has temporarily closed nine rides across the US and Canada as a precaution.

Here's what we know so far about the incident.

The Cobb County Police Department said the incident at the Six Flags Over Georgia park happened just before 16:00 local time (20:00 GMT) on Monday.

"Officers working at the park responded to an incident involving a male guest on a roller coaster," it said in a statement on Tuesday.

"Preliminary information gathered through witness and employee interview indicates Kariem was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction."

The ride involved has not been specified but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, and multiple witnesses have identified the ride as the one involved in the incident.

The office of the state's insurance and fire safety commissioner, which enforces amusement park safety rules in Georgia, is also conducting a review.

Officials have not held a news conference on the incident.

The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five.

The company said in a statement that it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident" and that "our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones".

Nick Mendenhall said he witnessed the fatal moments in disbelief, watching the man come out of his seat and then fall into another cart on the ride before falling to the ground.

"It was just super, super bizarre, traumatic. I mean, it took me a couple of seconds, I feel like, to process what was going on," he told the AP. "I cant believe that I just saw that."

He said his mind instantly went to the trauma of all of those impacted by what he witnessed, including the man's loved ones and everyone who was on the ride with him.

One witness told NBC affiliate WXIA that the incident was captured in souvenir photos that were automatically taken of the rollercoaster while it was in motion. The BBC has not been able to verify this statement.

Connor Thompson told the BBC's US partner CBS News that he was in line for the ride when everyone started "yelling, clearly distressed".

"Everyone was kind of confused at first, and then there was someone who was yelling, 'Call 911! Someone fell out!" he said. "At first it was almost like I didn't believe it because I thought that was like impossible for something like that to happen."

He said he saw the cart come into the hub where others were waiting in line and could see the restraint was unlatched.

Another witness, CiCi Nelson, told CNN she, too, was in line to ride the Goliath when the rollercoaster returned and she saw an empty seat with a loose safety bar and a female covered in blood.

Nelson described a scene of hysteria, adding that one man was "freaking out, saying someone fell off".

Brittany Landry, who believed she saw Kariem ejected from the rollercoaster, told Fox News she was in tears.

"I broke because we were just on there," she said.

Who is the victim Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem?

Kariem's family said he was a father, passionate educator and had survived two bouts of cancer.

His family told WXIA that he had survived cancer twice - the last stint in 2018 - and was in a car crash with his 10-year-old daughter three weeks before his death.

He lived in the nearby city of Atlanta and worked for Wesley International Academy, a public charter school, for more than 12 years as an IT manager, technology teacher and robotics coach.

"Mr. Kariem was deeply loved and respected, and his absence will be felt throughout our school community," the school said in a statement posted to its Facebook account.

"His love for Wesley, dedication to our students, and commitment to our school community were evident in everything he did."

Outside of work, Kariem enjoyed creating products with his laser engraver and 3D printers, as well as cooking, watching anime and spending time with family and friends, according to his profile on the school's website.

The death at Six Flags Over Georgia is at least the seventh there, according to the Doan Law Firm, which tracks amusement park accidents and represents victims.

According to the firm, this includes two people who had medical emergencies, two who were in restricted areas when they were struck by a ride, two who died in car-related accidents and one who died months after using the park's pool.

Six Flags operates 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico.

In the last 15 years, two deaths caused by falling from the park's rollercoasters led to lawsuits and settlements. One in 2011 involved an Iraq War veteran who was ejected from a ride in New York and hit his head on the car. In the other, in 2013, a woman slipped from her restraints on a rollercoaster in Texas and fell 75 feet.

In September, the Six Flags Magic Mountain park in California announced it was closing its X2 rollercoaster after more 100 people alleged that they had suffered brain injuries from the ride.

articles.title: Namibia battles cattle disease outbreak as EU suspends several meat imports
articles.summary: Foot-and-mouth disease threatens livestock farmers’ livelihoods and disrupts meat supplies as authorities impose curbs.
articles.body:
Windhoek, Namibia – “We had to close the market for several days. It was just before the weekend and month’s end. That’s when we need the money the most,” says Francisco, a vendor at Single Quarter, Windhoek’s largest open meat market.

He pours vinegar and cooking oil into a tomato and onion salsa, a traditional accompaniment to kapana, a popular grilled-meat street food. Around him, many stalls and grilling stations sit empty. Instead of the crowds that typically fill the market during business hours, only a handful of customers move between the stalls.

Recent closures and concerns about meat supplies have disrupted business.

“Our business is slow. We are struggling to buy meat, but without it, we cannot survive,” says another kapana vendor, who asked to remain anonymous. “This is our livelihood. The meat is much more expensive now, so we are making less money altogether. If this continues for three months, it is going to be very bad for us.”

In Katutura, Windhoek’s largest township, uncertainty over beef supplies is adding to residents’ financial concerns.

“If we don’t eat meat, what are we going to eat? We are Namibians,” one resident says, describing meat as a staple of the local diet. Another worries about rising prices and the wider consequences for Namibia, where livestock exports are an important part of the economy.

At a supermarket in the Okuryangava suburb, the butchery has already run out of some premium beef products. Store manager Enrico De Azevedo, 23, says consumer behaviour has also contributed to the pressure.

“We saw people panic-buying like they did during the COVID-19 pandemic with toilet paper. Now, they can go and stack their meat next to their toilet paper,” he says.

De Azevedo also recognises the wider economic risks. “For those in the export business, this will have grave implications.”

Outbreak threatens Namibia’s export market

Namibia’s Directorate of Veterinary Services (DVS) confirmed an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) on a commercial farm in the Karasburg State Veterinary District, in the southern //Kharas Region, on September 23, 2026.

In an address on October 5, President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah said surveillance teams had recorded 127 positive cases across 15 farms. Teams had inspected 29,313 animals across 68 farms. The government had also established 20 surveillance teams and 10 roadblocks in the region as part of its response.

In an update covering the situation as of October 6, the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform reported that 129 animal samples had tested positive and 17 farms had been confirmed infected. Veterinary teams had inspected 72 of 81 targeted farms.

The outbreak was subsequently confirmed in a second region. On October 7, laboratory tests confirmed FMD in cattle at Kalala Island, in the Kabbe constituency of the Zambezi Region, in northern Namibia.

Veterinary officials from the Katima Mulilo State Veterinary Office investigated the suspected outbreak on October 5 after observing clinical signs in 20 cattle. Twelve samples were collected and submitted to the Central Veterinary Laboratory in Windhoek on October 6. All 12 tested positive for the virus the following day.

In a public notification issued on October 10, the ministry outlined restrictions across the Zambezi Region following confirmation of the outbreak.

These include suspending the movement of cloven-hoofed animals and their raw products, cancelling previously issued movement permits, and halting livestock auctions, informal markets and other animal-gathering events. Slaughter at local abattoirs, informal markets and social events has also been suspended.

Slaughter at export abattoirs may continue for eligible cattle under the commodity-based trade system, provided the animals meet quarantine requirements and pass traceability checks.

Emergency vaccination has begun in the affected area, while roadblocks and intensive surveillance are intended to prevent further spread.

FMD is a highly contagious viral disease affecting cloven-hoofed animals, including cattle, sheep, goats and pigs. It can disrupt livestock production and trade, particularly when it affects areas recognised as free of the disease.

Following confirmation of the //Kharas outbreak, Namibian authorities notified the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) and introduced restrictions on the movement and export of cloven-hoofed animals and their products.

The European Union subsequently amended its import rules for Namibia’s previously authorised export zone, known as NA-1, following the outbreak.

The Zambezi detection has added to the challenge facing veterinary authorities, who are working to contain the disease and prevent further infections. The available information confirms outbreaks in both regions but does not establish that the disease spread directly from //Kharas to Zambezi.

“The outbreak has been a heavy blow to our country,” Marianne Pretorius, head of communications at the Namibia Agricultural Union (NAU), told Al Jazeera by email. “The restrictions are painful, but they are necessary, and the NAU supports them.”

On October 5, the European Union announced a temporary suspension of entry into the bloc of specified fresh meat products from cattle, sheep and goats, as well as certain products from other farmed and wild hoofed animals, from Namibia’s previously authorised export zone. The restrictions also cover specified processed meat products, including biltong and jerky.

The measure is not a blanket suspension of all Namibian meat imports. According to the EU, certain processed products that undergo the prescribed risk-mitigating treatment remain eligible for entry. Qualifying fresh-meat consignments certified by Namibian authorities before September 23 may also enter during a 90-day transitional period, subject to the applicable EU rules and border-control requirements.

The restrictions apply to the specific products covered by the EU measure. It remains unclear whether the Zambezi outbreak will affect exports to other markets or under other trade arrangements.

For the country’s livestock industry, the restrictions add to the uncertainty created by domestic movement controls and the loss of access to some export markets.

“For farmers in the //Kharas region, the impact is immediate and severe, but this is not only a //Kharas problem,” Pretorius said. “When export markets close, every livestock producer in the country feels it.”

She warned that the consequences could continue even after domestic trading resumes.

“Even when domestic trade resumes, prices may remain under pressure until export markets reopen,” she wrote. “That is why we are calling for market recovery to be treated with the same determination as disease control.”

Containment measures expand as economic costs mount

Namibia has stepped up efforts to contain the disease, including plans to strengthen veterinary fencing in high-risk areas.

Construction of a veterinary cordon fence along the Orange River in the //Kharas Region began in October. The barrier is intended to strengthen controls along the border with South Africa. The government has also pursued additional fencing and containment measures in high-risk areas.

The containment measures are intended to limit animal movement and reduce the risk of further infections. Their effectiveness will depend on surveillance, compliance with movement restrictions and the ability of veterinary authorities to identify and contain new cases.

The outbreak is also affecting the country’s meat-processing sector. The Namibian reported on October 12 that Meat Corporation of Namibia (Meatco) had placed about 400 production workers on three weeks of special leave with full pay. The situation was due to be reviewed on October 23, with workers’ return depending on guidance from veterinary authorities.

The Namibian also reported that Meatco had paid farmers N$31 million (about US$1.8 million) for cattle delivered to its Windhoek abattoir between August 29 and September 11. The payments cover cattle already delivered, while uncertainty remains over future sales and export access.

For livestock producers, the outbreak threatens immediate income and the longer-term viability of their businesses. Restrictions on moving and selling animals can interrupt cash flow even for farmers whose herds have not been infected.

Gert Engelbrecht, a 40-year-old farmer from Aranos, said the restrictions had created financial and emotional strain for producers.

“Our livestock is not simply a business to us; it is our livelihood and something we have invested our lives in,” he told Al Jazeera. “Being able to move and sell livestock is fundamental to keeping the farming operation going. It affects farmers across Namibia when movement and markets are restricted. Ultimately, we need to regain our disease-free status.”

The DVS has intensified surveillance and is tracing livestock movements that took place before the outbreaks were detected.

For farmers, restoring market access is essential to keeping their operations running. Meat vendors, meanwhile, depend on reliable supplies to sustain their businesses.

“Farmers are fighters,” Engelbrecht said. “We understand why restrictions are necessary, but we are not sitting back and waiting for somebody else to solve this. We are working with the veterinary authorities to see this disease controlled, regain our status, and restore access to our markets.”
